entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Palais Garnier (Paris Opéra or Opéra Garnier), completed in 1875 after 15 years of construction and designed by Charles Garnier at age 35, is the most lavish opera house ever built — a Second Empire Baroque confection of marble, gilded bronze, and painted ceilings covering 11,000 m² that became the architectural symbol of Napoleon III's Paris transformation. It is the most famous opera house in the world, the largest in capacity, and the setting for Gaston Leroux's The Phantom of the Opera (1910) — with an actual underground lake beneath the building.

Napoleon III commissioned Georges-Eugène Haussmann's transformation of Paris (1853-1870), which required a new opera house as centerpiece. The young architect Charles Garnier won the competition over 170 entrants, defeating the Empress Eugénie herself (who preferred a neo-Gothic competitor). Garnier's design — a synthesis of eclectic Baroque ornament, Beaux-Arts planning, and industrial engineering — took 15 years (1860-1875) and cost 36 million gold francs. The Grand Staircase, decorated with 30 types of marble, is one of the most theatrical architectural spaces in the world.

The underground lake — 6 meters deep — is not fictional: it was built as counterweight for the hydraulic stage machinery and genuinely exists. Leroux used it as basis for the Phantom's lair. The Chagall ceiling (1964, painted over the original) was controversial but is now beloved — Chagall's colorful mural covering the original ornate ceiling. The Palais Garnier receives 1.5 million visitors annually (more as museum than opera venue since the Bastille Opéra opened in 1989).

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Palais Garnier — the most lavish theater ever built and the setting of The Phantom of the Opera — defines what an opera house can mean culturally: it is simultaneously the apex of 19th-century theatrical architecture and the world's most mythologized musical theater setting.
